results.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search?
results.answer: Binary search is O(log n) time complexity. Each step eliminates half the remaining elements, so for a sorted array of n items you need at most ⌈log₂n⌉ + 1 comparisons. Space is O(1) for the iterative version, O(log n) for the recursive one (call stack).

results.prompt: is it worth learning Rust this year?
results.answer:
I couldn't search for the latest data right now, so this is from what I know and may be a bit dated. But the core answer hasn't changed: it depends on what you're learning it for.

- For a generalist or career move: yes, if you can spend a few hours a week. Rust has been the "most loved" language in the Stack Overflow surveys for years, and demand is real in systems, embedded, WebAssembly, and infra teams. It's a strong differentiator on a CV.
- For your day-to-day work: only if it fits. If you mostly do web front-end or data/Python work, the payoff is lower — you'll spend a lot of time fighting the borrow checker for skills that don't compound much.
- For fun and fundamentals: it's one of the best languages to learn, period. The ownership model rewires how you think about memory and concurrency in a way that makes you a better programmer in other languages too.

My pick: learn it this year, but set a concrete goal — a small project, or contributing to something you use — instead of "learning Rust" vaguely. The borrow checker is a wall; a project gives you a reason to climb it.

results.prompt: tell me something interesting about octopuses
results.answer:
I've got a good one: octopuses are one of the few animals with three hearts. Two pump blood to the gills, and the third handles the rest of the body — but here's the twist: that third heart actually stops beating when the octopus swims. Swimming is so energetically expensive that their body shuts it down, which is why octopuses prefer crawling and only swim when they're in real trouble.

A couple more that tend to surprise people:

- Their blood is blue, because it uses copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen instead of the iron-based hemoglobin we have.
- They have nine "brains" of sorts — one central brain plus a kind of mini-brain in each arm, which is why an octopus arm can keep working and even react to touch after being cut off.
- They can taste with their suckers, so they literally sample everything they touch.
